title: Guiding Data Allocation for Robust Subpopulation Generalization
topic: Data-centric AI->Data-centric AI methods and tools
claim: Many diverse, even highly imbalanced, training configurations match or beat the balanced one, and simplex projection with gradient directions makes this explorable.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, matrix and arrow linking histogram to 3D simplex plots
description: Three panels. (a) is a blue histogram of Waterbirds-syn test accuracy over many training configurations, with a red dashed vertical line marking the balanced configuration's accuracy. Much of the mass sits at or above that line. (b) shows a grouped bar chart of group ratios for four groups, comparing the balanced configuration (dark blue) with two skewed examples (light blue and orange). A grey arrow labeled 'Simplex Projection' carries a 4x3 matrix that maps the ratio vector to 3D coordinates. A 3D plot of a dashed tetrahedron follows, with colored dots for Example 1, Example 2 and the simplex center. (c), after a dashed divider, shows another tetrahedron with solid (Grad) and dashed (Bal) arrows pointing toward the center. The eye goes first to the histogram, then the bars, then the 3D simplices.
caption: {} (a) Test accuracy varies over diverse training data configurations and many match or exceed the performance of the balanced configuration. (b) Data configurations visualized by projecting group sizes onto a 3-simplex, including the configurations for the balanced (center), the highly skewed (vertex), and a random configuration (unique coordinate). (c) Visualization of directions estimated according to the gradients (Grad) and balancing (Bal) towards the center.
abstract: Machine learning models often achieve high average accuracy in the training data while performing poorly on test data due to subpopulation shift. A common data-centric solution is to enforce balanced subgroup proportions, but full balance can be costly, infeasible, and not always necessary. In this work, we study whether balanced training data is the unique optimal configuration for robust subpopulation generalization. We extend a Gaussian feature-model framework to theoretically characterize the performance landscape across general training subgroup distributions. We show that multiple configurations, including substantially imbalanced ones, can perform comparably to the balanced one. We further derive gradient-based directions for adjusting subgroup proportions to improve adjusted accuracy and worst-group accuracy more efficiently. These findings suggest that strategically allocating data offers a more flexible and principled path to robust performance than simple balancing. The code is available at https://github.com/zhaoyingpan/subpop-data-allocation.
